summary.text:
A strategy unusually explicit about its rules. Paragraph 5.6 sets dated trigger rates for new PWLB borrowing (4.50% this year, 4.25% in 2026/27, 4.0% in 2027/28), §4.11 prints the full MUFG interest rate view with its 22 December date on it, and the balance sheet ties across all five years of the strategy — CFR less external borrowing less other long-term liabilities equals the paper's own internal-borrowing row exactly, in every year.

Two things join up. Internal borrowing is planned to fall from £90m at 31 March 2026 to £40m by 31 March 2029 — a £50m run-off funded from new external borrowing — while £43.2m of the existing PWLB book matures within 12 months of 31 December 2025 and the loans-maturities chart at §8.1 puts a ~£60m lump into 2027. That is on the order of £100m of external borrowing decisions to be taken inside about two years, all against the trigger rules above. On the DMO's certainty curve on 14 August, no maturity printed below the 4.50% current-year trigger; the cheapest point (1y at 4.95%) sat 45bp above it, and against the 4.25% 2026/27 trigger the gap widens to 70bp. The MUFG view had 5-year PWLB reaching 4.30% by September; actual was 5.34%.

The MRP policy at §3 anchors the annuity method to 'the prevailing PWLB interest rate for a loan with a term equivalent to the estimated life of the project', so the rate printed by us at the moment 2025/26 capex becomes MRP-bearing (from 2026/27 per §3.3) will lock the annuity for the asset's life. Financing-cost ratio starts at 17% and eases to 14% across the strategy as net revenue grows faster than financing cost. The Appendix names no officer with an email address — that lives in the Cabinet covering report, which we do not hold. The PWLB loan-book reconciliation does not hold at 31 December (our file records ~£302m less than the paper prints); the loan-file start-date issue is the most likely cause and the claim is kept out of the email.

contacts.note: No officer named with an email address anywhere in the Appendix. The Cabinet covering report (10 February 2026) would carry a Contact Officer front sheet but is not held here. Advisor listed is MUFG Corporate Markets (§1.7).

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026-29 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Full Council on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is unusually explicit — dated trigger rates, an interest rate view labelled with the exact day it was struck, and prudential indicators that balance across every year of the forecast — and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Your paragraph 5.6 sets explicit trigger rates for new PWLB borrowing: 4.50% for anything drawn this year, 4.25% for 2026/27 and 4.0% for 2027/28. That is one of the clearest borrowing rules we have read, and it is testable. On the DMO's certainty curve at Thursday's PM fixing (notice 314/26), the cheapest point on the entire PWLB curve was the 1-year at 4.95% — 45bp above your current-year trigger. 5-year certainty was 5.34%, 10-year 5.83%, 25-year 6.46%, 50-year 6.27%. None of the standard maturities prints below 4.50% today, and against your 4.25% trigger for the next financial year the gap widens to 70bp at the cheapest point.

The MUFG rate view your Appendix prints at §4.11 was made on 22 December, and expected 5-year PWLB to reach 4.30% by September. What has actually happened since is around 100bp in the other direction over that maturity. We don't publish forecasts, deliberately, and we're not going to offer you one. What we do publish is the SONIA-implied forward path for each PWLB maturity, updated daily against wherever the last stated forecast sat, so the point at which a stated trigger becomes reachable is a number that can be watched rather than inferred.

The other side of this is your internal-borrowing pathway. Indicator 5 has internal borrowing running down from £90m at 31 March 2026 to £40m by 31 March 2029 — a £50m reduction over three years, replaced from new external borrowing — while gross debt rises about £38m across the strategy. On top of that, £43.2m of the existing book was within 12 months at 31 December, and the loans-maturities chart at §8.1 puts a lump of around £60m into 2027. Combined, that is on the order of £100m of external borrowing decisions to be taken inside about two years, all against the trigger rules above. The sector-lending breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July's activity was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, thin volume when a book of this size needs feeding.

One thing from the paper worth noting back. Your MRP policy at §3 sets the annuity charge against 'the prevailing PWLB interest rate for a loan with a term equivalent to the estimated life of the project'. That prevailing rate is the one we publish daily at each maturity — and §3.3 delays the MRP charge for 2025/26 capex to 2026/27, so the rate observed at the moment MRP begins will lock the annuity for the asset's life. Not something to act on, but the sort of number worth being able to see move.

On training, three courses fit. Reading the PWLBpredict is the obvious one given the trigger rules and the December forecast. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, because the internal-borrowing run-off is the point at which the benchmark tells you when capacity actually runs out. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, since §6.4(a) contemplates rescheduling should the opportunity arise. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
